hypothesis: An adversary who compromised Windows hosts in this network stole credentials from them (MITRE ATT&CK tactic: Credential Access).

assessments.reason: PsExec-delivered payload that spawned the credential-file harvester, Rar.exe and sdelete64.exe.
Password-protected archiving of harvested credential files, then wiped.
Anti-forensic deletion of Rar.exe and both working.zip copies.
Azure guest log collection; its lsass 0x10 access is standard.
Run by pbeesly PowerShell from attacker-staged SysinternalsSuite during credential access.
Lateral movement to NASHUA with cleartext pbeesly credentials running python.exe.
Wiped the staged screen-saver, Draft.Zip and SysinternalsSuite.zip.
Defender service; lsass 0x10 access is normal scanning.
Oddly named screen saver in C:\ProgramData\victim launched by explorer; wrote monkey.png decoded by a hidden IEX stager.
Compiled qkbkqqbs.dll and 0piklvia.dll from PowerShell response files in Temp.
Started with -verb runas by PowerShell, followed by registry-stored encoded stager execution.
Three launches from cmd.exe just before payload compilation; known execution proxy, no credential access seen.

frame.restated: An adversary with existing access to Windows hosts on this network is stealing credentials from those hosts.
frame.what_would_confirm: Observable evidence such as LSASS process memory access (e.g., via Mimikatz or procdump), suspicious access to SAM/SECURITY registry hives, use of Windows Credential Manager APIs, or anomalous authentication events indicating credential theft.
frame.what_would_refute: Absence of any credential dumping tool execution, no unauthorized access to LSASS or registry hives, and no anomalous credential-related events on the compromised Windows hosts.

verdict.rule: Confirmed if >=1 in-scope incident of verified malicious findings (confidence >= medium); Inconclusive if only suspicious incidents or coverage gaps; Refuted if full coverage and no malicious/suspicious finding

T1003.name: OS Credential Dumping
T1003.reason: Credential-access toolset executed on both hosts; no dump file observed.

T1003.001.name: LSASS Memory
T1003.001.reason: Audited powershell.exe LSASS handle open (0x10) on scranton.

T1003.002.name: Security Account Manager
T1003.002.reason: All SAM_SERVER/SAM_DOMAIN/SAM_ALIAS handle requests are by lsass.exe as SCRANTON$; no reg save or hive copies; SAM/SECURITY file hits were Prefetch .pf files.

T1003.003.name: NTDS
T1003.003.reason: No ntds.dit access, ntdsutil/vssadmin/diskshadow command lines or shadow-copy activity; only WerFault crash dumps.

T1003.004.name: LSA Secrets
T1003.004.reason: No SECURITY Policy Secrets object access, lsadump or secrets-related command lines/script blocks.

T1003.005.name: Cached Domain Credentials
T1003.005.reason: HKLM\SECURITY\Cache\NL$1 writes are performed by lsass.exe itself (normal cached-credential updates); no mscache/DCC2 extraction.

T1003.006.name: DCSync
T1003.006.reason: No drsuapi/dcsync/lsadump references in process command lines or PowerShell script blocks.

T1040.name: Network Sniffing
T1040.reason: No sniffing artifacts in any dataset: zero hits for tcpdump/windump/wireshark/rawcap execution, pcap/sniff/promiscuous command lines, Npcap/WinPcap driver loads (sysmon event 6), or capture-driver service installs (7045 shows only PSEXESVC and a Java support service). The high-volume hits are benign Azure infrastructure (NetworkWatcherAgent.exe, logman.exe stop GAEvents under WaAppAgent.exe). The malicious PyInstaller python.exe on nashua makes rapid outbound TCP to 192.168.0.4:8443 (C2/scanning), not passive packet capture. Zeek window does not overlap and shows no ICMP conn records.

T1056.name: Input Capture
T1056.reason: Input-capture tooling present (Keystroke-Check script, python.exe payload via PsExec) and anomalous all-access LSASS handles from PowerShell/wsmprovhost; baseline LSASS/SAM access otherwise benign.

T1056.001.name: Keylogging
T1056.001.reason: Keystroke-Check AV-evasion function in psversion.ps1 on scranton and remote deployment of C:\Windows\Temp\python.exe (PyInstaller, pywintypes/win32pipe) to nashua via PsExec with cleartext credentials, opening cmd/powershell with PROCESS_ALL_ACCESS.

T1056.002.name: GUI Input Capture
T1056.002.reason: No 4104 script blocks or 4688 command lines referencing Credential/Prompt/Read-Host were found (checks C076/C080 returned zero hits).

T1056.003.name: Web Portal Capture
T1056.003.reason: No file writes to wwwroot/inetpub/login, no w3wp/iis process activity, no 4663 access to web content, and no HTTP POST or login/portal URLs in zeek (checks C084/C086/C087/C089/C091 zero hits).

T1056.004.name: Credential API Hooking
T1056.004.reason: PowerShell.exe (0x1f3fff, 0x1fffff) and wsmprovhost.exe (0x1f3fff) opened lsass.exe with full access via PowerShell cmdlet call traces on scranton/nashua; no explicit hooking DLL evidence, so suspicious rather than confirmed.

T1110.name: Brute Force
T1110.reason: Zero 4625/4740/4771 events in windows.security; the only 4776 (newyork, pbeesly) returned Error Code 0x0. No authentication-failure or lockout pattern exists.

T1110.001.name: Password Guessing
T1110.001.reason: No failed logons and no password-bearing command lines; the single credential validation succeeded, consistent with normal domain logon.

T1110.002.name: Password Cracking
T1110.002.reason: LSASS accesses are dominated by svchost.exe (0x1000) and AV/Azure telemetry agents; full-access opens came from the pbeesly PowerShell loader, wsmprovhost and boot-time wininit/csrss. No SAM/SECURITY hive reads, no hash/crack tooling, no wordlist or potfile creation.

T1110.003.name: Password Spraying
T1110.003.reason: No spray pattern (no 4625s, no user-list command lines). The observed authentication activity is reuse of one valid credential (pbeesly) via PsExec64 to NASHUA, which is lateral movement rather than spraying.

T1110.004.name: Credential Stuffing
T1110.004.reason: No failed authentications across accounts from any source; 4648 events map to the pbeesly/PSEXESVC pair, the pbeesly RDP session from 172.18.39.2, and OS accounts.

T1111.name: Multi-Factor Authentication Interception
T1111.reason: No MFA-interception artifacts in any dataset: no smart-card/MFA credential-provider tampering, no 4104 script referencing Credential/MFA (C135 zero hits), no MFA proxy or token-theft tooling. The credential-related hits are benign OS behaviour (CredentialGuard scenario value set to 0x0 by lsass.exe, CredentialEnrollmentManagerUserSvc service keys by services.exe, DWM/UMFD/SCRANTON$ 4648 logon plumbing) plus attacker credential ACCESS by pbeesly on nashua (wsmprovhost.exe opening lsass.exe with 0x1f3fff while running Get-Process -IncludeUserName, and PsExec 4648 logons) — that is credential dumping/enumeration, not MFA interception.

T1187.name: Forced Authentication
T1187.reason: On scranton.dmevals.local, DMEVALS\pbeesly PowerShell tooling (Invoke-Exfil in psversion.ps1) mapped \\192.168.0.4\webdav with explicit credentials via New-PSDrive; Sysmon shows powershell.exe and svchost.exe (WebClient) connecting to 192.168.0.4:80, and Zeek shows the same host 10.0.1.4 falling back from rejected SMB 445/139 to WebDAV OPTIONS/PROPFIND with Microsoft-WebDAV-MiniRedir/DavClnt user agents — the forced-authentication/WebDAV coercion pattern. Remaining 5140/5145 and SMB hits are benign SYSVOL/IPC$ domain traffic.

T1212.name: Exploitation for Credential Access
T1212.reason: On scranton.dmevals.local, PowerShell.exe (PID 2976) opened lsass.exe with GrantedAccess 0x1F3FFF and 0x1FFFFF at 2020-05-02T03:05:16Z with an ntdll/KERNELBASE/UNKNOWN call trace, inside a confirmed pbeesly intrusion chain (registry shell persistence, PNG-steganography shellcode loader, Invoke-Exfil 7-Zip+WebDAV exfil, hidden base64 PowerShell). A second, lower-confidence LSASS handle by wsmprovhost.exe on nashua.dmevals.local (0x1F3FFF, managed PowerShell call trace) is assessed suspicious; the remaining Kerberos and svchost/AV LSASS accesses are benign.

T1539.name: Steal Web Session Cookie
T1539.reason: No browser session-cookie theft found. The only cookie-named file creation is a LocalService package INetCookies file created by svchost.exe on scranton (03:21:05Z), and the only 'cookie' command lines are rundll32 davclnt.dll,DavSetCookie for the \\192.168.0.4\webdav WebDAV share used by the attacker's Invoke-Exfil script. No access to Chrome/Firefox/IE cookie stores, Login Data, WebCache or Local Storage files, and no cookie-related PowerShell script blocks or windows.other messages. Sysmon 10 access to Edge processes is normal Explorer/svchost IPC plus 0x1000 query-only access from PowerShell.

T1552.name: Unsecured Credentials
T1552.reason: Credential-named collection and password-protected archiving on nashua.

T1552.001.name: Credentials In Files
T1552.001.reason: Credential-named file harvesting on nashua and cleartext password on PsExec64 command lines.

T1552.002.name: Credentials in Registry
T1552.002.reason: All registry Password/Credential value sets came from svchost.exe, lsass.exe, services.exe and winlogon.exe performing normal identity/service/credential-guard plumbing.

T1552.003.name: Shell History
T1552.003.reason: No ConsoleHost_history.txt or other shell-history file access appeared in sysmon or security telemetry.

T1552.004.name: Private Keys
T1552.004.reason: LocalMachine private keys exported to .pfx and exfiltrated via WebDAV.

T1552.006.name: Group Policy Preferences
T1552.006.reason: No Groups.xml, cpassword or sysvol credential access; only routine GptTmpl.inf/gpt.ini writes and a NETWORK SERVICE gpupdate.exe /target:computer.

T1555.name: Credentials from Password Stores
T1555.reason: Certificate-store private keys exported; no browser/vault access seen.

T1555.003.name: Credentials from Web Browsers
T1555.003.reason: All browser credential-store checks (C209-C214) returned zero hits; collection on scranton targeted documents, certificates, keystrokes and clipboard instead.

T1555.004.name: Windows Credential Manager
T1555.004.reason: LSASS handle access is dominated by Windows/Azure platform binaries (svchost, wininit, csrss, MsMpEng, CollectGuestLogs, WindowsAzureTelemetryService, AntimalwareConfig); no cmdkey/vaultcmd/DPAPI Credential Manager access found. The non-platform LSASS access is attributed to the pbeesly intrusion reported under T1555.

T1555.005.name: Password Managers
T1555.005.reason: Checks C221-C226 for KeePass/1Password/Bitwarden/LastPass/kdbx artefacts returned zero hits on all hosts.

T1556.name: Modify Authentication Process
T1556.reason: SYSTEM-context PowerShell.exe (scranton, 03:05:16, 0x1F3FFF/0x1FFFFF) and wsmprovhost.exe (nashua, 03:09:29, 0x1F3FFF) opened full-access handles to lsass.exe during an APT29-style hands-on-keyboard intrusion (SysinternalsSuite drop, Invoke-Discovery, Invoke-Persistence, Get-PrivateKeys, Get-Keystrokes). No actual authentication-process patch was observed.

T1556.001.name: Domain Controller Authentication
T1556.001.reason: Type-3 logons are machine-account/loopback traffic; 4648 events are pbeesly via PSEXESVC.exe and winlogon. No Skeleton Key/injected-credential indicators, no LSA/SAM registry writes.

T1556.002.name: Password Filter DLL
T1556.002.reason: No Notification Packages/PasswordFilter registry change, no password-filter DLL file creation in System32, no matching command lines or script blocks.

T1556.005.name: Reversible Encryption
T1556.005.reason: No 4739, no Set-ADUser/dsmod/Reversible command lines, no reversible-encryption references in PowerShell or windows.other.

T1556.006.name: Multi-Factor Authentication
T1556.006.reason: No 4739/5136 authentication-policy or directory changes; registry writes in the window are notification/tile and W32Time values.

T1556.007.name: Hybrid Identity
T1556.007.reason: No 5136 changes and no Connect-MsolService/Connect-AzureAD script blocks; dsregcmd.exe only loaded cryptdll.dll.

T1556.008.name: Network Provider DLL
T1556.008.reason: No NetworkProvider/credential-provider registry writes; LSA key appears only in read-only 4656 handle opens (AccessMask 0x1).

T1557.name: Adversary-in-the-Middle
T1557.reason: No adversary-in-the-middle positioning found. The malicious activity on scranton.dmevals.local (pbeesly) is credential theft (certificate .pfx export, screen capture, 7z exfiltration) plus PsExec lateral movement to nashua with cleartext credentials and a masquerading javamtsup service — but no interception/relay of victim traffic.

T1557.001.name: Name Resolution Poisoning and SMB Relay
T1557.001.reason: SMB/Kerberos flows are normal member-to-DC authentication (10.0.1.4/10.0.1.6 -> 10.0.0.4 on 445/389/88, IPC$/sysvol mappings); DNS queries are ordinary with no LLMNR/NBT-NS poisoning, no DNS client registry tampering (4657 zero hits) and no Responder/relay tooling in script blocks.

T1557.002.name: ARP Cache Poisoning
T1557.002.reason: Zeek L2 stacking shows stable one-to-one MAC/IP mappings (00:0d:3a:13:e3:69, 00:0d:3a:4d:42:f2, fc:bd:67:e1:a9:c1) with no MAC claiming multiple IPs and no gratuitous/duplicate mappings; no arp/netsh manipulation in PowerShell.

T1557.003.name: DHCP Spoofing
T1557.003.reason: No DHCP telemetry exists: no DHCP event codes in windows.other, no dhcp log type in Zeek, no ports 67/68 in Sysmon network connections, and no Dhcp references in PowerShell script blocks.

T1558.name: Steal or Forge Kerberos Tickets
T1558.reason: No ticket theft/forgery, but PowerShell (pbeesly, PID 2976) on scranton.dmevals.local opened lsass.exe with 0x1f3fff/0x1fffff at 03:05:16Z right after discovery/persistence/certificate-export commands — credential access consistent with an active intrusion.

T1558.001.name: Golden Ticket
T1558.001.reason: All 4769 tickets are AES256 (0x12) with success status; krbtgt SPN requests are ordinary TGS; 4672 logons only by machine account NEWYORK$; no golden-ticket tooling in PowerShell.

T1558.002.name: Silver Ticket
T1558.002.reason: Service tickets target normal machine accounts/SPNs with AES256 and success; zeek shows routine cifs/host/ldap TGS requests; no silver-ticket tooling.

T1558.003.name: Kerberoasting
T1558.003.reason: No RC4 (0x17/0x18) service-ticket requests and no Kerberoast/Rubeus script blocks; all TGS use aes256-cts-hmac-sha1-96.

T1558.004.name: AS-REP Roasting
T1558.004.reason: AS exchanges show KDC_ERR_PREAUTH_REQUIRED followed by successful AES256 AS-REP for pbeesly, i.e. pre-auth enforced; no AS-REP roasting tooling observed.

T1606.name: Forge Web Credentials
T1606.reason: Private-key material collected and exfiltrated; no forged token observed.

T1606.001.name: Web Cookies
T1606.001.reason: No forged or tampered web cookies. The single cookie-store file event is a benign svchost.exe creation of a LocalService INetCookies file on scranton; no PowerShell cookie/session handling and no cookie-bearing forged requests in Zeek.

T1606.002.name: SAML Tokens
T1606.002.reason: No SAML/ADFS/token artifacts were observed (zero hits for SAML, NotOnOrAfter, Assertion, saml/adfs/token URLs). However, the attacker stole certificate private keys and performed full-access LSASS reads (PowerShell 0x1f3fff/0x1fffff on scranton, wsmprovhost 0x1f3fff on nashua), which are the prerequisites for minting forged SAML tokens.

T1621.name: Multi-Factor Authentication Request Generation
T1621.reason: No MFA/2FA/authenticator/push/duo/okta activity in any dataset. The 85 C355 hits in windows.other are WMI-Activity 5857/5858 provider-start and RSoP DeleteInstance records (ResultCode 0x80041002 / 0x0) by SYSTEM and NETWORK SERVICE, not authentication requests. windows.security has zero 4625 events, PowerShell 4104 blocks contain no MFA-related strings, Sysmon command lines contain none, dsregcmd only reached the local DC 10.0.0.4, and Zeek HTTP had no login/auth/mfa URLs.

T1649.name: Steal or Forge Authentication Certificates
T1649.reason: Export-PfxCertificate loop over cert:\LocalMachine then archive and exfil.

checks.purpose: Stack all process creations to spot credential-dumping tools (mimikatz, procdump, comsvcs.dll rundll32) among rare executables.
Stack process-access targets to find LSASS or other credential-store processes being opened.
Stack object types accessed under handle/object-access auditing to find SAM/SECURITY/LSASS objects.
Stack newly created processes to spot dumping utilities launched on hosts.

args.query: event.code:4104 AND (powershell.script_block_text:*lsass* OR powershell.script_block_text:*mimikatz* OR powershell.script_block_text:*sekurlsa* OR powershell.script_block_text:*DumpCreds*)

checks.purpose: Find PowerShell script blocks referencing LSASS/credential-dumping APIs.
Look for credential-dumping references in other Windows event channels (service installs, VSS, etc.).
Stack granted-access masks on LSASS process opens to reveal memory-read access typical of dumping.
Read individual LSASS access events with source image and granted access.

findings.title: PowerShell process opened LSASS with full-access masks (0x1F3FFF / 0x1FFFFF) on scranton

The call trace ends in UNKNOWN modules (ntdll.dll+9c584|KERNELBASE.dll+2732e|UNKNOWN(...)), i.e. code not backed by a known on-disk module. All other LSASS opens in the dataset are svchost.exe with 0x1000/0x1400 (benign), so these two are the only memory-read-class accesses.

findings.title: PowerShell and wsmprovhost opened LSASS with full access (0x1f3fff / 0x1fffff) on scranton and nashua
findings.summary: Sysmon event 10 shows C:\windows\system32\WindowsPowerShell\v1.0\PowerShell.exe (PID 2976, scranton) requesting GrantedAccess 0x1f3fff and 0x1fffff on lsass.exe at 03:05:16Z, and wsmprovhost.exe (PID 7720, nashua) requesting 0x1f3fff on lsass.exe at 03:09:29Z with a call trace through System.ni.dll / Microsoft.PowerShell.Commands.Management.ni.dll (i.e. a PowerShell cmdlet, not a native API). These are the only non-system processes in the dataset with all-access LSASS handles; the remaining LSASS opens are svchost 0x1000, Azure telemetry/antimalware 0x1400 and OS boot processes (wininit/csrss). The all-access LSASS handles coincide with the pbeesly intrusion chain (Keystroke-Check script, PsExec to nashua, python.exe payload), consistent with credential/API-hooking style access to LSASS memory.

On scranton.dmevals.local, user DMEVALS\pbeesly ran a PowerShell toolkit (loaded from C:\Program Files\SysinternalsSuite\psversion.ps1) that defines Invoke-Exfil. The scriptblock maps a network drive to the UNC path \\192.168.0.4\webdav with explicit credentials (cozy / MyCozyPassw0rd!) via New-PSDrive and copies $env:APPDATA\OfficeSupplies.7z to it. Sysmon shows powershell.exe (PID 3852, DMEVALS\pbeesly) initiating TCP/80 to 192.168.0.4 at 2020-05-02T03:08:47Z, followed by svchost.exe (LOCAL SERVICE) connections to 192.168.0.4:80 at 03:08:50Z and 03:10:23Z — the WebClient/WebDAV redirector behaviour that turns a UNC path into HTTP. In the Zeek window (2020-04-30, non-overlapping) the same host 10.0.1.4 is seen probing 192.168.0.4: SMB 445/139 rejected (REJ) at 00:32:14–00:32:18Z, then WebDAV HTTP with user agent Microsoft-WebDAV-MiniRedir/10.0.18362 and DavClnt issuing OPTIONS/PROPFIND to /webdav, /webdav/OfficeSupplies.7z and /webdav/python.exe (00:32:18–00:32:21Z and 00:35:25Z). This is the forced-authentication/WebDAV coercion pattern (SMB blocked, fallback to WebDAV over HTTP) used to push credentials to an attacker-controlled listener. The same host also set HKCU Folder\shell\open\command to a hidden PowerShell one-liner and later ran Invoke-SeaDukeStage against NASHUA, so the activity is clearly attacker-driven, not administrative.

findings.title: PowerShell on scranton.dmevals.local opened lsass.exe with full-access masks (0x1F3FFF / 0x1FFFFF) during a hands-on-keyboard intrusion by user pbeesly
findings.summary: On scranton.dmevals.local, PowerShell.exe (PID 2976, running as SYSTEM per the Sysmon event's AccountName) opened the lsass.exe process (PID 736) twice within 31 ms at 2020-05-02T03:05:16Z with GrantedAccess 0x1F3FFF and 0x1FFFFF — PROCESS_ALL_ACCESS-class rights that permit reading credential material from LSASS. The call trace is ntdll.dll+KERNELBASE.dll followed by an UNKNOWN module, i.e. not a normal Windows component. This is not isolated: the same host/user pbeesly shows a full intrusion chain in the same window — registry Folder\shell\open\command persistence (02:57), a bitmap-steganography loader that decodes a PNG into shellcode and IEXs it (02:58:45), SysinternalsSuite.zip expansion (03:00), an 'Invoke-Exfil' script block that 7-Zips the Downloads folder with password 'lolol' and copies it to \\192.168.0.4\webdav using hardcoded credentials (03:08), and a hidden base64-encoded powershell -nop -w hidden -e launch (03:21:28). The lsass access is therefore part of malicious post-exploitation, consistent with exploitation/abuse of the credential store rather than any legitimate tooling. Note: the 0x1FFFFF accesses by wininit.exe/csrss.exe at 03:19:09 coincide with a SYSTEM logon type 0 (boot) and are normal boot-time behaviour; the svchost 0x101001/0x3000 accesses are likewise service-manager activity. Only the PowerShell-sourced accesses are attributed as malicious.

This is direct private-key theft.

findings.summary: On 2020-05-02 between 03:03 and 03:08 UTC, in the context of user DMEVALS\pbeesly on scranton.dmevals.local, an interactive PowerShell session (PID 3876) renamed a dropped file readme.txt to readme.ps1, dot-sourced it, and then executed a function Get-PrivateKeys that enumerates every certificate in cert:\LocalMachine recursively and exports each one with its private key to $env:USERPROFILE\Downloads\<random>.pfx protected by the hardcoded password "saribas" (Export-PfxCertificate). Sysmon recorded the resulting file C:\Users\pbeesly\Downloads\coyn5igj.3io.pfx created by that same powershell.exe PID 3876 at 03:04:57, and the same PowerShell process wrote the certificate store blobs HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\SystemCertificates\MY\Certificates\48B5E43D09D080DF8863152FD22ED7C43443D499\Blob and ...\Remote Desktop\Certificates\615B93C2D2B647D1670500B3338EAAEC83BA5646\Blob at 03:04:57. The exported .pfx was later deleted at 03:08:51 by another powershell.exe (PID 3852) under pbeesly, consistent with staging/cleanup after theft. The same session also ran screen-capture and clipboard-collection functions, indicating a broader hands-on-keyboard intrusion. This is theft of authentication certificates/private keys (T1649), not normal system behaviour.

findings.summary: On 2020-05-02 the sysmon LSASS-access stack (326 events) is dominated by svchost.exe (289, GrantedAccess 0x1000) plus Azure antimalware/telemetry agents (0x1400). The rare outliers are PowerShell.exe (PID 2976) on scranton.dmevals.local at 03:05:16 requesting 0x1F3FFF and 0x1FFFFF on lsass.exe (PID 736), and wsmprovhost.exe (PID 7720) on nashua.dmevals.local at 03:09:29 requesting 0x1F3FFF on lsass.exe (PID 728), both running as SYSTEM. These full-access handles are the prerequisite for reading/patching the authentication process. They occur inside a hands-on-keyboard intrusion on scranton: SysinternalsSuite was downloaded/expanded to C:\Program Files\SysinternalsSuite, readme.txt renamed to readme.ps1 and dot-sourced, then Invoke-Discovery, Invoke-Persistence -PersistStep 1/2, Get-PrivateKeys, Get-Keystrokes and Get-Clipboard were executed. No evidence of an actual LSASS patch, password filter, or authentication DLL replacement was found, so this is suspicious credential-access staging rather than confirmed authentication-process modification.

findings.title: No network sniffing observed; PyInstaller python.exe on NASHUA is C2/scanning, not packet capture
findings.summary: The T1040 hypothesis is not supported by the telemetry. Across windows.security (460 4688 events), windows.sysmon (447 process-create events) and windows.powershell (414 4104 script blocks) there is no tcpdump/windump/wireshark/rawcap execution, no pcap/sniff/promiscuous command line, no Npcap/WinPcap driver load (event 6), and no capture-driver service installation. The 7045 service installs are PSEXESVC (from PsExec) and a Java support service, not capture drivers. The two high-volume 'network tool' candidates are benign infrastructure: NetworkWatcherAgent.exe (Microsoft Azure Network Watcher plugin, registry/file activity on nashua, scranton, utica) and logman.exe ("logman.exe" stop GAEvents, parent C:\WindowsAzure\Packages\WaAppAgent.exe — Azure guest agent telemetry). The genuinely malicious-looking activity in this window is on nashua.dmevals.local: a PyInstaller-packed C:\Windows\Temp\python.exe dropped at 03:10:23Z and launched four times via PsExec64 from scranton (03:11:40, 03:12:46, 03:13:49, 03:15:03Z) using cleartext credentials dmevals\pbeesly, preceded by PowerShell 'Invoke-SeaDukeStage -ComputerName NASHUA'. That binary extracts _MEI29522 with _socket.pyd/_ssl.pyd and opens hundreds of rapid outbound TCP connections from 10.0.1.6 to 192.168.0.4:8443 — this is C2/scanning behaviour, not passive sniffing, so it does not satisfy T1040. The zeek window (2020-04-30) does not overlap the Windows window and shows no ICMP conn records; its top destination 192.168.0.4 is ordinary traffic. Note: the python.exe activity is malicious in nature but belongs to other techniques (execution/lateral movement/C2), not network sniffing.

findings.title: No shell history access observed
findings.summary: No process creation or file-access event referencing ConsoleHost_history.txt or other shell history files was returned in any dataset. The attacker's PowerShell activity was captured through script-block logging rather than history-file reads.

findings.title: No Group Policy Preferences credential extraction observed
findings.summary: No process command line or file-access event referenced Groups.xml, sysvol, or cpassword in the Windows datasets. The only GroupPolicy-related file activity was routine GptTmpl.inf/gpt.ini writes under the local GroupPolicy DataStore, and gpupdate.exe /target:computer was run by NETWORK SERVICE, which is normal policy refresh behaviour.

findings.title: No browser credential-store access (Login Data / logins.json / browser process handles) on any host
findings.summary: Checks C209-C214 (Sysmon process/file/process-access, Security object access, PowerShell script blocks, other channels) for browser credential files and browser process handles returned zero hits across scranton, nashua, newyork and utica. The intruder's collection on scranton targeted documents, certificates, keystrokes, clipboard and screenshots rather than browser password databases; no evidence of web-browser credential theft in this window.

findings.title: LSASS handle access on all four hosts is dominated by Windows/Azure platform binaries — no Credential Manager (vault/cmdkey) theft observed
findings.summary: Stacking the 326 Sysmon event-10 LSASS accesses shows 293 with 0x1000 and 24 with 0x1400, produced by svchost.exe, services.exe, csrss.exe, wininit.exe, wsmprovhost.exe, dsregcmd.exe, RuntimeBroker.exe, ShellExperienceHost.exe, sppsvc.exe, wmiprvse.exe, MsMpEng.exe, WindowsAzureTelemetryService.exe, AntimalwareConfig.exe and CollectGuestLogs.exe — normal Windows/Azure guest-agent behaviour. Security 4663/4656 object-access on lsass.exe likewise comes from CollectGuestLogs.exe (0x1410/0x10) and MsMpEng.exe. The only non-platform LSASS access is the pbeesly PowerShell/wsmprovhost activity reported under T1555. No cmdkey, vaultcmd, DPAPI Protect folder or Credential Manager file access was found (checks C217-C220 returned nothing beyond a benign 'Credential Guard configuration: 0x0, 0' event on scranton).

findings.title: No password-manager artefacts (KeePass/1Password/Bitwarden/LastPass/kdbx) observed
findings.summary: Checks C221-C226 for password-manager executables, files, process handles, command lines, script blocks and other-channel messages returned zero hits on all four hosts. The only credential-adjacent collection seen was certificate private-key export (Get-PrivateKeys writing .pfx files) and keystroke/clipboard capture by pbeesly on scranton, which is not password-manager store access.

findings.title: Network logons are machine-account and PSEXESVC activity; no DC authentication backdoor observed
findings.summary: The 218 type-3 logons are almost entirely the NEWYORK$ machine account authenticating from ::1, fe80::e40c:95b6:b0a7:6429 and 10.0.0.4, i.e. normal local/loopback machine-account traffic. The 15 explicit-credential (4648) events show user pbeesly using explicit credentials from 10.0.1.6 on scranton and via C:\Windows\PSEXESVC.exe on nashua, plus a DWM-1/winlogon.exe entry — consistent with PsExec administration, not with a Skeleton Key or injected false credentials on a domain controller. No 4657 registry change to LSA/SAM and no 4688 command line referencing lsass/cryptdll/msv1_0 were found.

findings.title: No password filter DLL installation or Notification Packages registry change
findings.summary: Checks for password-filter indicators returned nothing: no 4657 change to Notification Packages/Password/lsass registry values, no 4688 command line containing Notification or PasswordFilter, no PowerShell script block referencing Notification/PasswordFilter/lsass, and no sysmon file-create of a DLL into System32. The only image loads into authentication DLLs are Microsoft-signed system DLLs (cryptdll.dll, samcli.dll, samlib.dll, msv1_0.dll, samsrv.dll) loaded by svchost.exe, lsass.exe, WmiPrvSE.exe, SearchIndexer.exe, LogonUI.exe and VSSVC.exe, plus one apisampling.dll load by svchost.exe on scranton at 03:21:27 (Microsoft 'API Sampling', 10.0.18362.1).

findings.title: No reversible-encryption or AD user-attribute modification observed
findings.summary: No 4739 (domain policy change), no 4688/sysmon process creation with Set-ADUser, dsmod or Reversible in the command line, and no PowerShell script block or windows.other message referencing AllowReversiblePasswordEncryption/ReversibleEncryption. The only account-related activity in the window is the pbeesly explicit-credential use described above.

findings.title: No MFA/authentication policy registry or directory changes
findings.summary: No 4739 policy-change events, no 5136 directory-object modifications, and no Set-ADUser/Set-ADAccountControl style command lines in sysmon or PowerShell. The registry writes seen on scranton between 03:04 and 03:10 are unrelated Windows notification/tile data and W32Time SecureTimeLimits values written by lsass.exe, not authentication-policy changes.

findings.title: No hybrid-identity (Azure AD / AD FS / Seamless SSO) tampering observed
findings.summary: No 5136 directory changes and no PowerShell script blocks referencing Connect-MsolService, Connect-AzureAD or similar hybrid-identity cmdlets. dsregcmd.exe on newyork.dmevals.local at 03:06:14 only loaded cryptdll.dll, which is normal for device-registration queries; no configuration change followed.

findings.title: No Network Provider DLL registration or credential-provider modification
findings.summary: No 4657 registry change to NetworkProvider or credential-provider keys and no PowerShell script block referencing NetworkProvider or New-ItemProperty. The LSA registry key (\REGISTRY\MACHINE\SYSTEM\ControlSet001\Control\Lsa) appears only in 4656 handle-open events with AccessMask 0x1 by pbeesly's cmd.exe/powershell.exe/conhost.exe on scranton and by LOCAL SERVICE svchost.exe on nashua — read-only key opens, not value writes.

findings.title: No name-resolution poisoning or SMB relay observed; SMB/Kerberos traffic is normal domain-member to DC authentication
findings.summary: The SMB and name-resolution telemetry shows only expected domain behaviour. Zeek SMB sessions are between internal members (10.0.1.4 scranton, 10.0.1.6 nashua) and the domain controller 10.0.0.4 (NEWYORK) on 445/389/88, mapping \\NEWYORK.dmevals.local\IPC$ and \sysvol, with Kerberos/GSSAPI authentication — consistent with GPO/SYSVOL access and machine-account logons (4624 type 3 as SCRANTON$/NASHUA$/UTICA$/WEC$). Sysmon DNS queries (81 events) contain only normal names (wpad, _ldap._tcp SRV lookups, microsoft/akamai/azure endpoints) with no LLMNR/NBT-NS-style single-label lookups answered by an unexpected host. No 4657 DNS client registry tampering, no Responder/LLMNR/NBT-NS script content, and no SMB relay listener was found. The 4697 service installs are the attacker's own javamtsup/PSEXESVC services (covered under T1557), not relay infrastructure. The one unusual SMB pattern — 10.0.1.4 -> 10.0.1.6:445 at 00:35:26 with source MAC fc:bd:67:e1:a9:c1 — is the attacker's PsExec SMB session to nashua, not a relay.

findings.title: No ARP cache poisoning indicators; MAC-to-IP mappings are stable and consistent
findings.summary: Zeek L2 address stacking over 613 conn records shows three source MACs (00:0d:3a:13:e3:69, 00:0d:3a:4d:42:f2, fc:bd:67:e1:a9:c1) and responder MACs 12:34:56:78:9a:bc (the gateway/DC side) plus broadcast ff:ff:ff:ff:ff:ff for NetBIOS 138 broadcasts. Each host MAC maps to a single consistent IP (10.0.1.4, 10.0.1.6) with no MAC claiming multiple IPs and no duplicate/gratuitous mappings that would indicate ARP spoofing. The 138/137 traffic is ordinary NetBIOS name-service broadcast from System. No PowerShell content referencing arp or netsh interface manipulation was found. The only external-looking flows (10.0.1.4 -> 192.168.0.5:1234 and :443) are the attacker's own C2/beacon traffic from the compromised host, not traffic redirected by ARP poisoning.

findings.title: No DHCP spoofing activity; no DHCP events or DHCP traffic in any dataset
findings.summary: No DHCP-related evidence exists in the collected windows. The System channel (windows.other, 216 events) contains no DHCP client/server event codes (1341/1342/1020/1063 returned zero hits), no PowerShell script block references Dhcp, and Sysmon network connections show no DHCP ports 67/68 — the destination-port stack is dominated by 8443, 389, 88, 53, 135, 445, 443 with no 67/68 entries. Zeek contains no dhcp log type (only conn, files, ssl, x509, dce_rpc, http, dns, kerberos, dpd, smb_files, weird, smb_mapping, notice, pe). The 5156 inbound-filter check also returned nothing. DHCP spoofing is therefore not observable in this telemetry and no indicator of it was found.

findings.title: Golden ticket: no forged-TGT indicators; krbtgt service-ticket requests are normal AES256 TGS renewals
findings.summary: All 28 event 4769 records on newyork.dmevals.local use Ticket Encryption Type 0x12 (AES256) with Failure Code 0x0 and Ticket Options 0x60810010/0x40810000 — no RC4 (0x17/0x18) downgrade, no anomalous encryption, no 4672 logons by unexpected principals (the 4672 events are the machine account NEWYORK$ with its standard privilege set). The krbtgt service requests by pbeesly@DMEVALS.LOCAL (03:04:04Z) and SCRANTON$@DMEVALS.LOCAL (03:19:13Z) are ordinary TGS requests for the krbtgt SPN, not forged TGT use. No golden-ticket tooling or krbtgt references appear in PowerShell script blocks.

findings.title: Silver ticket: no service-ticket forgery indicators; TGS requests are routine host/SPN access
findings.summary: The 4769 service tickets on newyork.dmevals.local target machine accounts (NEWYORK$, NASHUA$, SCRANTON$, WEC$) and krbtgt, all AES256 (0x12) with success status 0x0, issued to pbeesly@DMEVALS.LOCAL and SCRANTON$@DMEVALS.LOCAL from 10.0.1.4/10.0.1.6. Zeek kerberos records (2020-04-30 window) show only AS/TGS requests by pbeesly for krbtgt, cifs/NEWYORK, cifs/NASHUA, ldap/NEWYORK and host/nashua with aes256-cts-hmac-sha1-96 and no failures other than normal KDC_ERR_PREAUTH_REQUIRED. No silver-ticket tooling or SPN-targeted script blocks were found.

findings.title: Kerberoasting: no RC4 service-ticket requests or roasting tooling observed
findings.summary: No 4769 ticket used RC4 (all 28 are 0x12/AES256), which is the hallmark of Kerberoasting, and no PowerShell script block referenced Kerberoast/Invoke-Kerberoast/Rubeus. The zeek kerberos log shows only AES256 TGS requests for cifs/host/ldap SPNs by pbeesly, consistent with normal file-share and host access.

findings.title: AS-REP roasting: no pre-auth-disabled account enumeration; AS exchanges are normal
findings.summary: Zeek kerberos AS exchanges from 10.0.1.4 and 10.0.1.6 to the KDC 10.0.0.4 are all for pbeesly/dmevals requesting krbtgt, each preceded by a normal KDC_ERR_PREAUTH_REQUIRED and followed by a successful AES256 AS-REP — i.e. pre-authentication is enforced, so no AS-REP roasting. No GetNPUsers/AS-REP/DontRequirePreAuth strings appear in PowerShell script blocks.

findings.title: No forged web cookies observed; only benign INetCookies file creation and ordinary HTTP traffic
findings.summary: The only cookie-related file event in the whole window is a single Sysmon file-create on scranton.dmevals.local at 2020-05-02T03:21:05Z by C:\windows\System32\svchost.exe writing C:\Windows\ServiceProfiles\LocalService\AppData\Local\Packages\warp_jit_db4a1097-b484-4973-bbf2-a04208ecd4d4\AC\INetCookies - a LocalService package cookie store created by the normal Windows service host, not by the attacker's PowerShell session. No PowerShell script block in windows.powershell references cookie, Set-Cookie or session handling (zero hits), and the Zeek window (2020-04-30, non-overlapping with the Windows telemetry) contains only 62 ordinary HTTP records from 10.0.1.4 to 192.168.0.4 with no cookie-forgery indicators. The attacker's credential theft on scranton targeted certificate private keys, not browser cookies, so cookie forgery is not evidenced.

findings.title: No MFA request generation observed; C355 hits are routine WMI provider events
findings.summary: The only T1621 check with hits (C355, windows.other, 85 events) matched WMI-Activity events 5857/5858, not authentication failures. Event 5858 (49 events, 48 on newyork.dmevals.local) are IWbemServices::DeleteInstance calls against Root\Rsop\Computer RSOP_ExtensionStatus.extensionGuid entries by NT AUTHORITY\SYSTEM with ResultCode 0x80041002 (object not found) — normal Group Policy/RSoP WMI cleanup. Event 5857 (36 events across newyork, scranton, nashua, utica) are WMI provider start records (dsccore, CIMWin32, deploymentprovider, dnsclientcim, StorageWMI) with result code 0x0, hosted in wmiprvse.exe. Neither is an MFA push/OTP request. No 4625 failed-logon events exist in windows.security, no MFA/2FA/authenticator/push/duo/okta strings appear in any of the 414 PowerShell 4104 script blocks, and no such strings appear in Sysmon process command lines (the only 'azure' matches were legitimate Azure guest-agent binaries such as WindowsAzureGuestAgent.exe, WaSecAgentProv.exe and NetworkWatcherAgent.exe). dsregcmd.exe on nashua.dmevals.local contacted only the local domain controller 10.0.0.4 on 389/135/49667, with no cloud identity-provider traffic. Zeek HTTP had no login/auth/mfa URLs. Separately noted but unrelated to T1621: C:\Windows\Temp\python.exe (SHA256 43782EC4337D8F3DDB7EA0C451B3BC4F212F84C8D5571BD0A842001C859A02AE) was launched as user pbeesly on nashua.dmevals.local via C:\windows\PSEXESVC.exe and made 348 TCP connections to 192.168.0.4:8443 — this is lateral-movement/credential tooling, not MFA fatigue.

findings.title: Routine certificate-store writes by lsass/svchost/taskhostw and Kerberos TGT requests are benign
findings.summary: The remaining T1649 hits are normal Windows certificate-store maintenance and normal Kerberos logons. On nashua.dmevals.local, lsass.exe (PID 728) wrote AuthRoot\Certificates\A8985D3A65E5E5C4B2D7D66D40C6DD2FB19C5436\Blob at 02:59:37 and svchost.exe wrote AuthRoot\Certificates\AFE5D244A8D1194230FF479FE2F897BBCD7A8CB4\Blob at 03:16:19 (root certificate auto-update); svchost.exe on nashua and scranton wrote Windows Live ID Token Issuer certificate blobs at 03:05; smss.exe wrote the WOW6432Node SystemCertificates SymbolicLinkValue on scranton at 03:19; taskhostw.exe wrote per-user ACRS PhysicalStores values for SID ...-1107 on scranton at 03:20. The single 4657 on nashua (ROOT\Certificates\BE36A4562FB2EE05DBB3D32323ADF445084ED656, subject NASHUA$, process C:\Windows\Sysmon.exe) is a machine-account store update, not attacker tooling. The 14 Kerberos 4768 TGT requests on newyork.dmevals.local are for pbeesly (9) and the machine account SCRANTON$ (5) from internal addresses 10.0.1.4/10.0.1.6 — ordinary interactive and machine logons, with no certificate-based (PKINIT) or forged-ticket indicators. The Zeek x509 subjects (rempel.group.net 376, conn.sons.info 2) are from a non-overlapping 2020-04-30 window and show no relation to the Windows hosts.

incidents.title: LSASS memory access with full-access masks by PowerShell on scranton
incidents.rationale: All describe the same action: PowerShell.exe (PID 2976) on scranton.dmevals.local opened lsass.exe with GrantedAccess 0x1f3fff/0x1fffff at 2020-05-02T03:05:16Z (plus the 4663 audit record of the same handle open). F10/F34 also include the nashua wsmprovhost LSASS open, but the dominant shared action is the scranton LSASS full-access open, which best fits T1003.001 (LSASS Memory).

incidents.title: PowerShell LSASS full-access open during hands-on-keyboard intrusion (T1212 framing)
incidents.rationale: Describes wsmprovhost.exe on nashua opening lsass.exe with 0x1F3FFF; the observed action is LSASS memory access, best fit T1003.001 (finding itself notes no dump payload observed, hence suspicious).

incidents.title: No Kerberos ticket theft/forgery; LSASS handle access by PowerShell on scranton
incidents.rationale: Finding reports no ticket theft/forgery; the only credential-access-shaped action is PowerShell opening lsass.exe with full-access masks on scranton, T1003.001.

incidents.title: No SAML token forgery; LSASS access by PowerShell/wsmprovhost
incidents.rationale: Finding reports no SAML/token artifacts; the observed credential-material theft is LSASS full-access access by PowerShell/wsmprovhost, T1003.001.

incidents.title: Keystroke-Check AV-evasion function and remote keylogger deployment to nashua
incidents.rationale: Describes the Keystroke-Check function and Get-Keystrokes keylogger deployment; the credential-access action is keylogging, T1056.001.

incidents.title: WebDAV/UNC forced-authentication exfil path from scranton to 192.168.0.4
incidents.rationale: Describes the Invoke-Exfil WebDAV/UNC path with explicit credentials and the powershell.exe connection to 192.168.0.4; the credential-access-relevant action is forced authentication via UNC/WebDAV, T1187.

incidents.title: Credential-access tooling staged on scranton (Sysinternals, keylogger, exfil scripts)
incidents.rationale: Both describe the staging and running of the Sysinternals toolset (accesschk, PsExec64, sdelete64) and credential/exfil scripts from C:\Program Files\SysinternalsSuite on scranton; the shared action is staging unsecured credential-access tooling, best fit T1552.

incidents.title: Attacker tooling staged in C:\Windows\Temp on nashua
incidents.rationale: Describes staging of python.exe, Rar.exe, sdelete64.exe in C:\Windows\Temp on nashua; unsecured credential-access tooling staging, T1552.

incidents.title: Credential-named file harvesting and archiving on scranton and nashua
incidents.rationale: Both describe enumeration of credential-named files (*psw*, *pass*, *login*, *admin*, *vpn) and archiving to Draft.Zip/working.zip on scranton and nashua; credentials in files, T1552.001.

incidents.title: accesschk.exe creating passwordsDB in SysinternalsSuite directory
incidents.rationale: Describes accesschk.exe creating a 'passwordsDB' file; credential material in files, T1552.001.

incidents.title: Cleartext pbeesly password on PsExec64 command lines to NASHUA
incidents.rationale: Describes cleartext credentials in PsExec64 command lines; credentials in files/command lines, T1552.001.

incidents.title: Get-PrivateKeys certificate private-key export to .pfx on scranton
incidents.rationale: All describe the same Get-PrivateKeys/Export-PfxCertificate action exporting cert:\LocalMachine private keys to a password-protected .pfx on scranton; private keys, T1552.004.

incidents.title: No password spraying; valid pbeesly credentials reused via PsExec64 to NASHUA
incidents.rationale: Finding explicitly reports no spraying; the observed action is credential reuse with PsExec to NASHUA, i.e. lateral movement (SMB/Windows Admin Shares), out of scope.

incidents.title: Credential-theft campaign on scranton with lateral SMB/PsExec movement to nashua
incidents.rationale: Finding reports no AiTM positioning; the described action spans credential theft plus lateral SMB/PsExec movement to nashua, whose best single fit is lateral movement, out of scope.

incidents.title: csc.exe compiling attacker .NET payloads from PowerShell response files
incidents.rationale: Describes csc.exe compiling attacker .NET payloads; this is execution (compile after delivery), out of scope.

incidents.title: No MFA interception; PowerShell Remoting logon-session enumeration on nashua
incidents.rationale: Finding reports no MFA interception artifacts; the observed action is PowerShell Remoting execution/enumeration by pbeesly on nashua, out of scope.

incidents.title: Screen-saver payload in C:\ProgramData\victim launched on scranton
incidents.rationale: Describes a malicious .scr screen saver executed by explorer spawning a PowerShell stager; this is execution/persistence, out of scope.

incidents.title: sdclt.exe execution proxy before payload compilation
incidents.rationale: Describes sdclt.exe execution proxy preceding payload compilation; this is execution/defense evasion, out of scope.

incidents.title: hostui.exe elevation attempt and registry-stored encoded PowerShell stager
incidents.rationale: Describes UAC bypass via hostui.exe runas and registry-stored encoded PowerShell stager; this is privilege escalation/execution, out of scope.
